title: Should Parents Approve Who You Marry?
paragraphs:
Should Parents Approve Who You Marry?
The Question That Has Broken Hearts, Divided Families, and Tested Faith—What Does God Actually Say?
There is a moment in almost every serious relationship when love collides with another voice.
Sometimes it is the quiet hesitation of a father.
Sometimes it is the tears of a mother.
Sometimes it is an entire family saying, "We don't approve."
And suddenly the question no longer feels theoretical.
Should parents approve who you marry?
Many have walked away from true love because of family pressure.
Others ignored every warning, married anyway, and discovered too late that wisdom had been speaking through people they refused to hear.
Some parents have become controlling.
Others have become prayer warriors.
Some children have honored their parents.
Others have confused honor with lifelong slavery.
So where does Scripture stand?
Not culture.
Not tradition.
Not modern romance.
Not personal opinion.
What does God actually say?
The answer may surprise you.
Because this is not merely a family issue.
It is a discipleship issue.
It is a question of authority.
It is a question of wisdom.
It is a question of whether Jesus truly rewrites every relationship—including the ones that hurt the most.
The Bible begins by establishing one of the greatest commandments ever given.
In Exodus 20:12 God commands:
"Honor your father and your mother..."
The Hebrew reads:

כַּבֵּד אֶת־אָבִיךָ וְאֶת־אִמֶּךָ
(Kabbed et-avikha ve'et immekha.)

The verb כַּבֵּד (kabbed) comes from כָּבֵד (kāḇēḏ), meaning "to make weighty," "to regard as significant," "to treat with great honor." Honor is not shallow politeness. It is recognizing the God-given value and role of one's parents.
The command is repeated in the New Testament.
Ephesians 6:2 says:
"Honor your father and mother."
The Greek reads:

Τίμα τὸν πατέρα σου καὶ τὴν μητέρα.
(Tíma ton patera sou kai tēn mētera.)
The verb τίμα (tíma) means to esteem, value, respect, and give proper honor.
Notice something important.
Scripture commands honor.
It never commands lifelong parental control over every decision of an adult child.
Honor is mandatory.
Absolute parental authority over a married adult is not.
Then comes Genesis.
One verse changes everything.
Genesis 2:24 says:
"Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh."
The Hebrew reads:
עַל־כֵּן יַעֲזָב־אִישׁ אֶת־אָבִיו וְאֶת־אִמּוֹ וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ
(Al ken ya'azov ish et aviv ve'et immo vedavaq be'ishto.)
The word יַעֲזָב (ya'azov) means "leave," not in the sense of abandoning or dishonoring, but of establishing a new primary covenant relationship. Marriage creates a new household under God.
Then comes וְדָבַק (vedavaq).
It means "cling," "cleave," "hold firmly," "be permanently joined."
Marriage is not merely romance.
It is covenant.
The priority shifts.
Parents remain honored.
The spouse becomes the closest earthly relationship.
Jesus Himself quoted this exact passage in Matthew 19:5, affirming that marriage creates a new covenant ordained by God.
This means something profound.
Parents are incredibly important.
But they are not the final authority over whom a mature believer marries.
God is.
However...
That truth has also been abused.
Some people say, "God told me to marry this person," while ignoring every warning from wise parents, pastors, mature believers, and Scripture itself.
That is not faith.
That is often pride wearing spiritual language.
Proverbs 15:22 reminds us:
"Without counsel plans fail, but with many advisers they succeed."
God frequently speaks through wise counsel.
Many parents see dangers that love refuses to notice.
Manipulation.
Addiction.
Abuse.
Financial irresponsibility.
Spiritual compromise.
Character flaws hidden behind attraction.
Parents have lived longer.
Many have already survived mistakes their children have yet to experience.
Ignoring godly wisdom simply because it feels inconvenient is never biblical.
But neither is allowing fear to replace obedience.
Sometimes parents oppose a marriage for reasons God never does.
Different social status.
Different ethnicity.
Different income.
Different church traditions.
Different expectations.
Human preferences must never override God's revealed truth.
The Pharisees were experts at elevating tradition above God's commands.
Jesus confronted them repeatedly.
The same danger still exists today.
The central biblical question is not:
"Do my parents like this person?"
Nor is it:
"Am I in love?"
The real question is:
Does this relationship glorify Christ?
Is this person surrendered to Jesus?
Are they producing the fruit of the Spirit?
Are they walking in repentance?
Do they display humility?
Can they lead—or help build—a Christ-centered home?
Will this marriage make both of you look more like Jesus?
Those questions matter infinitely more than chemistry alone.
Scripture repeatedly warns believers not to enter spiritually divided marriages.
Second Corinthians 6:14 says:
"Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers."
The Greek phrase is:

Μὴ γίνεσθε ἑτεροζυγοῦντες
(Mē ginesthe heterozygountes.)

The word ἑτεροζυγοῦντες (heterozygountes) describes animals yoked together that do not fit properly, making the work difficult and unstable. Paul's primary point concerns spiritual partnership and shared devotion to Christ. While the passage is broader than marriage, the principle has long been recognized as especially relevant to the closest covenant relationship.
Marriage was never designed merely to survive.
It was designed to reflect Christ.
Ephesians 5 tells us marriage points toward the relationship between Christ and His Church.
Every Christian marriage is meant to preach the Gospel without words.
That changes everything.
The question is no longer merely:
"Who makes me happy?"
Instead it becomes:
"Who helps me worship Jesus more faithfully?"
That question has saved countless marriages before they ever began.
The Bible gives us beautiful examples of parental involvement without portraying parents as infallible.

Abraham's servant sought a wife for Isaac under Abraham's guidance (Genesis 24), but the narrative also highlights God's providence and Rebekah's willingness. When Rebekah was asked whether she would go, she answered, "I will go" (Genesis 24:58). Her consent mattered.
Likewise, Scripture also records painful family failures.
Samson pursued relationships against wise counsel and against God's revealed purposes, with devastating consequences (Judges 14–16).
Yet there are also moments when faithful people followed God's calling despite misunderstanding from family.
The Bible never presents a simplistic formula.
Instead, it calls believers to wisdom, prayer, discernment, humility, and obedience to God.
If your parents love Jesus deeply, treasure their counsel.
Listen longer than your emotions want to.
Ask questions.
Invite correction.
Pray together.
If they raise concerns rooted in Scripture, take them seriously.
But if their objections are based solely on pride, prejudice, manipulation, or personal control, remember that your highest allegiance belongs to Christ.
Even Jesus taught that loyalty to Him surpasses every earthly relationship (Matthew 10:37). That does not cancel the command to honor parents; it establishes the proper order of every allegiance.
For parents reading this, remember that your children do not ultimately belong to you.
They belong to God.
Your role is not to control every decision.
It is to disciple, pray, counsel, bless, and entrust them to the Lord.
The strongest Christian families are not built on domination.
They are built on truth wrapped in grace.
And for those who have already made painful mistakes...
Perhaps you married against wise counsel.
Perhaps you ignored warning signs.
Perhaps your parents rejected someone they never should have rejected.
Perhaps your family relationships still ache today.
Hear this clearly.
The Gospel is not merely for perfect decisions.
The Gospel is for broken people.
Peter denied Christ.
David committed grievous sins.
The Samaritan woman carried the weight of shattered relationships.
Yet Jesus met each of them with truth and mercy, calling them to repentance and restoration.
That is why our message has always been:
He rewrites prodigals.
He rewrites broken marriages.
He rewrites stubborn hearts.
He rewrites controlling families.
He rewrites bitterness.
He rewrites regret.
He rewrites every surrendered life.

If you are still single, seek God's kingdom first. Pray for discernment. Invite wise, biblically grounded counsel. Honor your parents without making them your savior. Trust Christ above your emotions without despising the wisdom He often provides through mature believers.
If you are a parent, remember that the greatest gift you can give your children is not merely your approval but your example of faithful discipleship.
If this message challenged you, be honest before God.
If this article helped you understand God's Word more deeply, don't keep it to yourself.
One act of obedience today can echo through generations tomorrow.
